new_statements.quote: Figure 9.2 shows the main features of the first three tone categories in Tutsa. Fourth tone is a checked tone, with short duration relative to other tonemes, and an oral or glottal stop coda. What follows is a very early preliminary description. A number of segmental combinations have not been adequately recorded, and nothing has been recorded within carrier sentences. Contours in Tutsa differ considerably from many other Tangsa-Nocte varieties. [...] It is still a four-tone system and the etyma fall under the same category as with other Tangsa-Nocte varieties discussed here. [p. 242:] As with other varieties, this is a toneless sesquisyllabic affix and [...] it does not appear to significantly alter the tone of the stem.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tutsa is described as a lexical tone language with four tonemes (tone 1 mid falling with final breathiness, tone 2 high level, tone 3 mid/low falling, tone 4 checked/short with stop coda) on monosyllabic stems; nominalising prefixes /e0/, /a0/ are toneless minor (sesquisyllabic) syllables. The source says nothing about word stress: no stress rule, no claim of absence of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. For tone: author flags the description as very preliminary (one primary consultant plus 2013 recordings of a second speaker), no carrier-sentence data, intonation and sandhi not studied.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms (single words in elicitation, no carrier sentences); tone-bearing unit is the stem syllable; prefixes are toneless minor syllables. Nothing on phrase-level prosody for Tutsa.
new_statements.identity_note: van Dam's Tutsa data (glottocode tuts1235, ISO tvt) come from Mr. Tesam Pongte (primary consultant) and 2013 recordings of Mr. Ngongling Hanphuk of Thamjang village near Changlang Town, Changlang District; van Dam & Rahman 2022 sample Tutsa at Dewin and Hanphuk villages. Rekhung 1992 is noted by LaPolla as covering the Sabban area of Changlang Subdivision. Tutsa was administratively counted under Tangsa until the 2011 census (and under Nocte earlier, per Das 2022); linguistically van Dam places it closest to Nocte and to Phong (Ponthai) within a Tangsa-Nocte-Tutsa-Ollo continuum.

sources.citation: van Dam, Kellen Parker. 2023 [submitted 8 Oct 2018]. The tone system of Tangsa-Nocte and related northern Naga varieties. PhD thesis, La Trobe University. xviii+315 pp. (333 pp. PDF). doi 10.26181/21858474.v1
sources.note: Section 9.2 'Tutsa' (pp. 240-245) is a self-described 'very early preliminary description' of Tutsa tone only: four tones (1 mid falling breathy, 2 high level, 3 mid/low falling, 4 checked/short with oral or glottal stop coda); nominalising prefix /e0/ and /a0/ described as toneless sesquisyllabic affixes; intonation and sandhi not studied. No mention of word stress or accent for Tutsa anywhere in the thesis (the only 'stress' remarks, pp. ~140, concern emphasis/intonation in Muishaung).

sources.note: Morphosyntax (auxiliaries, copulas) with Tutsa examples from Khonsa fieldwork 2017; no tone marking, nothing on stress.

sources.citation: van Dam, Kellen Parker & Syed Iftiqar Rahman. 2022. Tangsa-Nocte as a Continuum: A diagnostic feature list for classification of varieties. Himalayan Linguistics 20(3). doi 10.5070/h920253557
sources.note: Segmental diagnostic features only (onsets of HAND, GRASS, WASH etc.); Tutsa villages sampled: Dewin, Hanphuk; says Tutsa is linguistically very close to Phong, Nocte and Muklom and that all Tangsa-Nocte varieties share a common four-tone system (citing the thesis). Nothing on stress.

sources.note: Three-page note on number and gender marking; states 'No study is found till now in a scientific way about the language'; nothing on phonology, tone or stress.

sources.note: The only full-length grammar of Tutsa; a Tezpur linguistics PhD almost certainly has a phonology chapter (ch. 2 or 3 of 9) that would state syllable structure, tone and possibly stress for Tutsa.
